metadata.note: Command teardown of ./art scenes and its aliases (scenes, scene, scene-search) — all three collapse into the same case branch in the top-level art dispatcher and exec runtime/scripts/scene_search.py. The middle body walks the 620-entry scene index built by build_scene_index.py, the four ranking rules (id > synonym > haystack, with IDF re-weighting for rare words), the --check anti-slate test, the --undocumented backfill list, and the automatic TEMPLATE-MISSES.md logging that catches a punt in flight. Falsifiability beat: the string 'yak shaving trombone' truly misses (exit 1) and the tool prints 'a miss is a PUNT, do not slate it.' All demo outputs in demo/RUN-LOG.txt are verbatim from this workspace against the isolated toolkit's scenes.json (620 renderable compositions after ClaudeCodeBeat916 was registered here for the portrait companion). Playlist adaptation for @HumanitariansAI: composer folder chip reads @HumanitariansAI; outro card is the locked ClaudeTitleOutro with hardcoded @NikBearBrown handle per OUTRO-LOCK.md — flagged for the human reviewer before publication. beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude UI cold open. Ask lands answered; narration introduces Liam in for Bear.
beats.narration_text: Namaste, this is Liam, in for Bear. There are six hundred and twenty renderable compositions in Brutalist. Nobody remembers them. So when you need a visual for a beat, the first move is not to author one. It is to search. Art scenes is the library-first check that stops a beat from being slated while a purpose-built component sits unused two directories away.

beats.role_note: FRAMEWORK — the shape of the dispatcher. One case branch, three aliases, one exec.
beats.narration_text: The dispatcher is a single case statement in the art file. One branch matches three aliases: the plural scenes, the singular scene, and the long form scene-search. All three exec the same python script. Different words in your terminal, one code path underneath.

props.title: art:67-70 — one branch, three aliases
props.code:
# From the top-level art dispatcher:
case "$cmd" in
  # ...
  scenes|scene|scene-search)
    # LIBRARY-FIRST: ask what already exists before
    # authoring, slating or punting a beat.
    exec python3 "$ART_HOME/runtime/scripts/scene_search.py" "$@"
    ;;
  # ...
esac
props.sparkLine: Three words. One script. One index.

beats.role_note: MECHANISM — the index. build_scene_index.py writes scenes.json; scene_search.py reads it.
beats.narration_text: The library the script searches is a single JSON file at runtime/remotion/src/scenes.json. Six hundred and twenty renderable compositions. Each record has an id, an aspect, a folder or group tag, a description, synonyms, and its props. That schema is what makes ranking possible — every record has the same shape, so the searcher can score them uniformly. The file is a build product, regenerated by art scene-index.

show.event: sample scene record types under it

props.title: runtime/remotion/src/scenes.json — the scene index
props.sparkLine: One schema. One ranking function. 620 leads.

beats.role_note: MECHANISM — the ranking. Three trust tiers, then IDF re-weighting so rare words win.
beats.narration_text: The ranker has one job: put the right lead at the top. Three trust tiers. An id hit is worth three points. A synonym hit is worth two. A hit anywhere else in the haystack — the description, the folder, the props — is worth one. Then it re-weights by inverse document frequency. That means a rare word like sankey outranks a common word like flow, so 'sankey flow' finds FinanceSankey and not every SourceFlow in the set. And a derived-only entry loses half a point, so a scene that actually describes itself outranks a guessed one.

show.event: three trust tiers type in as a bulleted block

props.title: scene_search.py — score()  (the ranker)
props.code:
def score(s):
    hay = hay_of(s)                # desc + when + folder + group + props
    n = 0
    for t in terms:
        if t in s['id'].lower():   n += 3 * weight(t)  # id      = high trust
        elif t in s['synonyms']:   n += 2 * weight(t)  # synonym = medium trust
        elif t in hay:             n += 1 * weight(t)  # haystack = low trust
    if s.get('desc_source') == 'derived':
        n -= 0.5                   # a described scene beats a guessed one.
    return n

# weight(t): rare word wins.
#   df <= 12 -> 2.0     df <= 60 -> 1.5     else -> 1.0
#
#   'sankey flow'      -> FinanceSankey  (not every SourceFlow in the set)
#   'bar chart'        -> BarChart       (id-hit outweighs every 'chart' entry)

beats.role_note: WORKED EXAMPLE — verbatim output of ./art scenes 'sankey flow' from this workspace.
beats.narration_text: Here is the shape on a real query. Dot slash art scenes quote sankey flow quote. Five candidates. Top of the list is FinanceSankey, scoring eight point five, because sankey is a rare word and it is right there in the id. The three source-flow scenes tie for second at four point five — same common word, spread across a bigger haystack. Every hit shows the id, the aspect ratio, the folder it lives under, and the props you can pass. That is enough to decide without opening a single file.

beats.role_note: WORKED EXAMPLE — --check and --undocumented. The anti-slate test and the backfill list.
beats.narration_text: Two more moves. Dash dash check is the anti-slate question — is this exact name renderable. It answers three things per name: renderable or not, aspect ratio, and the first six props you can pass. If you missed, it names the miss as a punt, because authoring a scene is a design card. Dash dash undocumented prints the backfill list — the one hundred and eighteen scenes whose search text was derived from file evidence because no one wrote a header sentence for them. Each of those is a small chore, and the tool shows you the pile.

props.title: --check (anti-slate)  and  --undocumented (the backfill)
props.code:
$ ./art scenes --check ClaudeComposerAsk BarChart NotAScene
  ClaudeComposerAsk       RENDERABLE   16:9   props: command, topic,
                                                     segment, greeting,
                                                     runningText, output
  BarChart                RENDERABLE   16:9   props: title, data,
                                                     accentIndex, unit
  NotAScene               NOT RENDERABLE - no <Composition> in Root.tsx.
                          Authoring this is a punt.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------

$ ./art scenes --undocumented
118 of 620 scenes run on DERIVED search text
(no header comment in the component):

  CodexComposerAsk          scenes/CodexComposerAsk.tsx
  CodexWindow               scenes/CodexWindow.tsx
  CodexCodeBeat             scenes/CodexCodeBeat.tsx
  ... 115 more

# Each needs one honest sentence at the top of its .tsx.
props.sparkLine: --check stops a slate. --undocumented is a chore list.

beats.role_note: WORKED EXAMPLE — the alias equivalence and the stop-word guard. Three different words, same answer.
beats.narration_text: One more receipt. Scenes, scene, and scene-search are not three commands. They are one command. Dot slash art scenes dash dash check, dot slash art scene dash dash check, and dot slash art scene-search dash dash check, on the same name, all print the same line. And a bare query of stop words — the, and, for, with — is rejected with a hint: search for the mechanic, not the sentence. The tool refuses to search on noise.

props.title: aliases + stop-word guard
props.code:
$ ./art scenes       --check ClaudeComposerAsk
$ ./art scene        --check ClaudeComposerAsk
$ ./art scene-search --check ClaudeComposerAsk

  ClaudeComposerAsk     RENDERABLE   16:9   props: command, topic,
                                                   segment, greeting,
                                                   runningText, output

# All three runs print BYTE-IDENTICAL output. The aliases are the case
# branch in art:67-70; they all exec the same script with the same argv.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------

$ ./art scenes "the and for with that this"
every word in that query is a stop word - search for the
mechanic, not the sentence.

# The stop-word guard refuses to rank on noise words like 'the',
# 'and', 'show', 'make', 'need' - 47 of them, hard-coded in QSTOP.
props.sparkLine: Same script, same output. Noise is refused.

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — the miss. The tool exits 1, prints a punt instruction, and appends to TEMPLATE-MISSES.md.
beats.narration_text: And here is what a real miss looks like. Yak shaving trombone. No scene matches. The tool does not silently return empty. It exits with status one. It prints an instruction: that is a PUNT — do not slate it, design the component, add it to the library. And it does one more thing that nothing else in the toolkit does. It writes the miss to TEMPLATE-MISSES.md with today's date, so the punt ledger does not depend on your discipline. A miss is a design card, filed automatically the moment it happens.

beats.role_note: VERDICT — the whole surface. One line each, in the order you actually use it.
beats.narration_text: So the surface. Bare art scenes prints the doctrine and exits. A query searches all six hundred and twenty compositions with the three-tier ranker and inverse document frequency. Dash dash check answers is-it-renderable. Dash dash undocumented lists the one hundred and eighteen scenes still owed a header sentence. Dash dash reel tags the miss to the reel that needed it. Dash dash no-log explores without polluting the ledger. Three aliases collapse to one code path. And a miss files itself in TEMPLATE-MISSES dot markdown.

props.artifactHeading: art scenes — the whole surface, in the order you actually use it
artifactLines: bare invocation — prints the doctrine (a hit is a lead, a miss is a punt) and exits 0.
"query" — searches all 620 compositions; id > synonym > haystack, IDF re-weighted; rare word beats common.
--check <Name...> — asks 'is that <Composition> in Root.tsx?' — the anti-slate test that stops one-off scenes.
--undocumented — lists the 118 scenes running on derived text; each needs a header sentence, then re-index.
--reel <path> / --no-log — tag misses with the reel that needed one; --no-log explores without polluting the ledger.
aliases scenes / scene / scene-search — same case branch, byte-identical output; one dispatcher, one code path.
a miss — no scene matches; the tool exits 1 and writes the query to TEMPLATE-MISSES.md as a design card.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — Your Turn composer. Prompt read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code from the brutalist toolkit root. It walks the whole surface: bare doctrine, three queries of different rarity, a check pair, the undocumented pile, and one deliberate miss with the reel tag. What you want to see is fair ranking on common words, the rare word winning where it should, a checked name coming back renderable, a checked typo coming back as a punt, one honest miss on your fake query, and identical output across the three aliases. If any run surprises you, that is a lead — file it against scene_search dot score.

props.segment: Audit art scenes on your own beat
props.command: From the brutalist.art toolkit root, run: ./art scenes; ./art scenes "bar chart"; ./art scenes "sankey flow"; ./art scenes "three-part funnel" --top 12 --no-log; ./art scenes --check ClaudeComposerAsk BarChart FormBCard NotAScene; ./art scenes --undocumented | head; ./art scenes "purely-made-up-thing" --reel youtube/your-reel. Then diff ./art scenes "BarChart" against ./art scene "BarChart" and ./art scene-search "BarChart" — all three must be identical. Finally, run the search on ONE beat you are authoring right now and record the top hit — or the miss.
output: top hits are relevant on common queries (bar chart, funnel)
rare word beats common word: 'sankey flow' finds FinanceSankey first
checks: three names IN SET, NotAScene is a punt
one honest miss on the made-up query — appears in TEMPLATE-MISSES.md
